The Tropical screech owl (Megascops trichopsis) is a small-bodied strigid inhabiting montane forests from southern Arizona through Central America. Data on its early development, informed by studies on the closely related eastern screech owl (Megascops asio), indicate that incubation under controlled thermal conditions yields a predictable hatching schedule. When eggs are maintained at a steady 36 °C [T = 36 °C], the incubation period lasts approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days], a duration typical for owls of this size range. Newly hatched nestlings exhibit a wet weight at birth of about 12 grams [Wwb = about 12 grams], a value that reflects the limited yolk reserves associated with the altricial developmental mode of this species. This initial mass is notably low relative to the adult body sizes these birds will eventually achieve, highlighting the considerable energetic investment required during the nestling phase.

As the nestling period progresses, the growing chicks undergo a rapid phase of mass gain, ultimately reaching distinct asymptotic body masses that differ between the sexes. Adult females attain a maximum recorded body mass of 94.4 grams [Wwi = 94.4 grams], while adult males, exhibiting the typical pattern of reverse sexual dimorphism common in many strigids, reach a smaller adult body mass of 83.7 grams [Wwi = 83.7 grams]. This sexual size dimorphism, where females are conspicuously larger, is thought to relate to their role in egg production and incubation. Under the thermal regime characteristic of active metabolic periods in this species, around 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], fledging occurs at 26 days after hatching [tx = 26 days after hatching]. The ability to achieve first flight and leave the nest after less than a month is a swift transition for an altricial bird of its relative size.

Sexual maturation in the Tropical screech owl follows a considerably longer timeline than the fledging process. Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and reproductive capability, is attained at 78 days after hatching [tp = 78 days after hatching], when the birds are still in a post-fledging, sub-adult stage at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This milestone is reached under the same standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] used for modeling life-history traits in related species. Despite achieving physiological sexual maturity relatively early in their lives, young individuals do not typically engage in breeding during their first year. Instead, a protracted period of deferred reproduction is observed, with the first successful breeding event occurring approximately 365 days after hatching [tR = approximately 365 days after hatching] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This delay is likely tied to the need to acquire a suitable territory and develop the hunting proficiency required to provision a brood.

Reproductive output in this species is modest, consistent with its life history as a tropical sedentary bird. Females typically lay between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch], and available records indicate they raise just a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year]. The annual reproductive output is thus constrained by both moderate clutch size and low frequency, a pattern that is further reflected in the long lifespan that allows for repeated breeding attempts over many years. Long-term banding studies provide an estimate of maximum longevity: under the standard thermal conditions of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the species exhibits a maximum lifespan of approximately 7,555 days [am = approximately 7,555 days], which compensates for the low annual fecundity.

Longevity studies based on banding and recapture data for the congener Megascops asio provide a useful comparative framework for understanding the Tropical screech owl's life history. Applying similar metabolic scaling assumptions at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the estimated maximum lifespan for M. trichopsis reaches approximately 7,555 days [am = approximately 7,555 days] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This remarkable longevity, spanning over two decades, is a classic feature of slow life-history species with low annual reproductive rates. The initial body mass of newly hatched chicks, measured at 14.1 grams [Ww0 = 14.1 grams], is slightly above the birth weight itself, a distinction that reflects the brief period of yolk absorption and early hydration before feeding begins. This value provides a baseline from which the subsequent growth trajectory toward the sexually dimorphic adult body masses can be modeled.
